summary: Collects best current practice examples of SIP call flows showing interworking with the public telephone network (PSTN). Scenarios include SIP to PSTN, PSTN to SIP, and PSTN to PSTN via SIP, with PSTN signaling illustrated using ISDN and ISUP. Elements include user agents, proxies and gateways.

plainLanguage.summary: This shows how an Internet phone call turns into a regular phone call and back. It follows each message step by step through the gateways that translate between the two worlds.

questions: how does a sip gateway map isup to sip
what is early media in sip
subtitle: Worked message-by-message examples of how SIP phone calls connect to, and through, the ordinary telephone network.

tldr.problem: Implementers building gateways between SIP networks and the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) need clear, reviewed examples of how the two signaling worlds line up message by message.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through scenarios in three groups (SIP to PSTN, PSTN to SIP, and PSTN to PSTN via SIP) showing each SIP message, each PSTN message (ISDN, ISUP or Feature Group B) and the gateway and proxy steps in between.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice companion to the SIP specification, with example flows rather than rules. The exact flows must not be copied as is.

today: RFC 3666 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 76) from December 2003, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It is a set of examples that accompanies RFC 3261 and RFC 3398, not a specification.

sections.title: Overview and Assumptions
sections.content:
The flows were developed in the design of a SIP IP communications network and represent an example of a minimum set of functionality. They are based on SIP 2.0 in RFC 3261, SDP usage from RFC 3264, and the SIP to ISUP mapping in RFC 3398. Basic SIP flows are in the companion RFC 3665.

The PSTN side is illustrated with ISDN, ISUP (ISDN User Part, mainly the ANSI variant) and FGB (Feature Group B) circuit associated signaling.

The assumptions are not requirements. Users are authenticated with HTTP Digest, some proxies insert Record-Route headers to stay in the signaling path, and transport may be TLS, TCP or UDP. The proxy does digit analysis and a location lookup to choose a gateway, normally with a primary and a secondary route. Gateways either play tones and announcements toward the PSTN from SIP responses, or pass in-band tones as early media toward the SIP side.
sections.plainLanguage: The book explains who is talking: phones, a helper that finds the right door, and translator boxes. They follow a few simple house rules, and the book says those rules are examples, not laws.

sections.title: Reading the Flows
sections.content:
In the diagrams, dashed lines (---) are signaling messages that are mandatory to the scenario, double dashed lines (===) are media paths, and a message name in parentheses is optional. Messages are labelled F1, F2 and so on, which point to the message details listed after each figure.

The cast is fixed. Alice (sip:alice@a.example.com) is a SIP phone, Bob is reached through the PSTN at the global number +19725552222, and Carol sits behind a PBX. A proxy server (Proxy 1) and gateways (NGW 1, NGW 2, GW 1 and so on) sit between them.

The RFC warns that the exact flows must not be copied as is. For readability the examples differ from real traffic: Digest responses are not real MD5 values, Call-IDs are often repeated, CSeq often starts at 1, and headers such as Accept, Supported and Allow are usually left out.
sections.plainLanguage: Each drawing is a comic strip of who says what to whom. The names are made up, and some details are simplified so the strip is easy to read.

sections.title: SIP to PSTN Dialing
sections.content:
Alice dials a number, and her SIP phone turns it into a global number inside a SIP URI. Proxy 1 picks a gateway. The gateway sends an ISUP IAM (initial address message) to Bob's switch, and a 183 Session Progress with SDP opens the early media path so Alice can hear ringing, busy tones or announcements. When Bob answers, ISUP ANM becomes SIP 200 OK. When Alice hangs up, her BYE becomes an ISUP REL.

The scenarios in this part are: a successful call to an ISUP PSTN number (2.1), a call to an ISDN PBX (2.2), a call with overflow (2.3), a call completed over IP after an ENUM query (2.4), and three failures (2.5 to 2.7).

In 2.3, NGW 1 answers 503 Service Unavailable, so Proxy 1 simply tries NGW 2. In 2.4, Alice's phone performs an ENUM query for 2.2.2.2.5.5.5.2.7.9.1.e164.arpa, gets back a NAPTR record with a SIP URI for Bob, and the call goes over IP without touching the PSTN.

In the first scenario the gateway returns sip:ngw1@a.example.com as its Contact, and that URI resolves to Proxy 1, because NGW 1 accepts SIP messages only when they come through the proxy.
sections.plainLanguage: Alice asks a helper to connect her to a regular phone. The helper picks a translator box, which rings the real phone. If the first box is busy, the helper just tries another one.

sections.title: When SIP to PSTN Calls Fail
sections.content:
Some failures end with in-band tones or recordings, such as busy tone or an announcement. The gateway sends 183 so the media path exists and Alice hears the final disposition. If Alice hangs up, she sends CANCEL rather than BYE, because no final response was ever received (2.5).

Other failures come back as an ISUP Release with a cause value. In 2.6, cause value 1 is mapped by the gateway to a SIP 404 response. In 2.7, the gateway's own timer expires when no ANM arrives, so it sends REL to the PSTN and 480 Temporarily Unavailable to Alice.

For the full cause-to-response mapping the RFC refers to RFC 3398.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the other phone is busy or never answers. Either you hear a busy sound through the line, or the translator box tells you with a plain message that it did not work.

sections.title: PSTN to SIP Dialing
sections.content:
Here the call starts on the PSTN. A switch sends an IAM to a gateway, which sends an INVITE to the proxy. The proxy forwards it to Bob's SIP phone. The SIP 180 Ringing becomes an ISUP ACM, and 200 OK becomes ANM. When the caller hangs up, ISUP REL is mapped to BYE.

The scenarios include a normal call (3.1), a fast answer where Bob sends 200 OK without any 180, so the gateway sends ANM without ACM (3.2), and a call from a PBX using Feature Group B signaling, where the gateway can identify only the trunk group (3.3). For ETSI and some other ISUP variants, a CON message would be sent instead of ANM.

Failures are covered too. A SIP error such as 604 or 600 Busy Everywhere is mapped to an ISUP REL with a cause value (3.4, 3.5). In 3.6 the response is turned into tones for the caller. In 3.7 and 3.8 the called party never answers: after a timer, Alice's network sends REL (cause code 102 Timeout in 3.8), which the gateway maps to CANCEL. 3.8 uses a stateless proxy. In 3.9 the caller abandons the call and REL becomes CANCEL. Had Bob answered after the REL, NGW 1 would have sent ACK and then BYE to terminate properly.
sections.plainLanguage: Now a regular phone calls an Internet phone. The translator box turns the phone-company messages into Internet messages and turns the answers back. If the Internet phone is busy or silent, it tells the phone company the right way.

sections.title: PSTN to PSTN via SIP
sections.content:
Both ends are ordinary telephone users, either PSTN subscribers or PBX extensions, and the call crosses two gateways and at least one proxy. The proxy authenticates and locates the gateways. A 183 Session Progress indicates that in-band alerting can flow from the called switch to the caller.

In 4.1 an ISUP call crosses SIP to another ISUP switch and completes normally. In 4.2 a Feature Group B PBX calls an ISDN PBX. Proxy 1 gets 503 Service Unavailable from GW 2, perhaps because all circuits are busy, and tries an alternative route via GW 3. The proxy uses the host part of the Request-URI to identify which private dialing plan applies.
sections.plainLanguage: Two regular phones can talk over the Internet in the middle. Each end has a translator box, and a helper finds a path between the two boxes, trying another if one is full.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The gateways in the examples are meant to follow the security considerations of RFC 3398. Mapping ISUP to SIP raises few concerns beyond privacy when the calling party number is passed on. Operators should use policies similar to those in PSTN switches.

Gateways should not trust the From header for identity, because users can fill it with anything. Cryptographic authentication and authorization should be used instead. Early media cut-through is needed for proper PSTN interaction but is also a risk, so operators need policies to prevent fraud and misuse. Even an authenticated user agent could send many simultaneous requests through a gateway, which would be a denial of service attack, so limiting simultaneous requests per entity is suggested.

No examples carry ISUP inside SIP bodies. The RFC notes that doing so raises abuse, fraud and privacy concerns, and says ISUP MIME bodies should be secured, preferably with S/MIME.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway must not believe a name tag just because the caller wrote it. It should check who people really are, and limit how many calls one person can start at once.
